section.title: Ministers of the New Covenant
section.sectionRationale: Paul answers the charge that he needs letters of recommendation by pointing to the Corinthians themselves as a living letter written by the Spirit on human hearts. This launches the letter's great meditation on the two covenants: the ministry of the letter engraved on stone, which came with a fading glory, and the ministry of the Spirit, which comes with a surpassing and enduring glory. The veil that lay over Moses' face and still lies over unbelieving hearts is removed only in Christ, so that with unveiled faces believers behold the Lord's glory and are transformed into His image.
section.thesis: God has qualified His servants as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter that kills but of the Spirit who gives life; the fading glory of Moses is eclipsed by the surpassing and enduring glory now revealed in Christ, and all who turn to the Lord have the veil removed and are transformed from glory to glory into His image.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Corinthians as a letter from Christ written by the Spirit; the surpassing glory of the ministry of the Spirit over the fading glory of the letter; and the veil removed in Christ so that with unveiled faces we are transformed into His image.

units.label: A letter from Christ
units.note: written by the Spirit on human hearts

verses.text: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you?
You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone.

It is clear that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the {{pneuma|Spirit}} of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
Such confidence before God is ours through Christ.
Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim that anything comes from us, but our competence comes from God.
And He has qualified us as ministers of a new {{diatheke|covenant}}, not of the {{gramma|letter}} but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

units.label: The surpassing glory of the new covenant
units.note: the fading glory of the letter and the enduring glory of the Spirit

verses.text: Now if the ministry of death, which was engraved in letters on stone, came with such {{doxa|glory}} that the Israelites could not gaze at the face of Moses because of its fleeting glory,
will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious?
For if the ministry of condemnation was glorious, how much more glorious is the ministry of righteousness!
Indeed, what was once glorious has no glory now in comparison to the glory that surpasses it.
For if what was fading away came with glory, how much greater is the glory of that which endures!

units.label: The veil removed in Christ
units.note: unveiled faces, transformed from glory to glory

verses.text: Therefore, since we have such a hope, we are very bold.
We are not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away.
But their minds were closed. For to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant. It has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed.
And even to this day when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts.
But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.
Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
And we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being {{metamorphoo|transformed}} into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. Here it is the Holy Spirit of the living God, who writes the new covenant not with ink on stone but on the living tablets of human hearts. Paul contrasts the Spirit who gives life with the letter that kills: the Spirit is the very power and glory of the new covenant ministry. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom, and by the Spirit believers are transformed into the image of Christ.

diatheke.gloss: Covenant, a binding arrangement that God Himself establishes and guarantees. Paul calls his ministry a ministry of a new covenant, the covenant promised in Jeremiah 31 in which God writes His law on the heart and gives His Spirit. Unlike the old covenant engraved on stone, the new covenant is inward, life giving, and enduring. It rests not on human competence but on God, who qualifies His servants and fulfils His promise in Christ.

gramma.gloss: Letter, the written character or code, standing for the law of Moses as an external written command. Paul says the letter kills: the law engraved on stone reveals sin and pronounces condemnation and death, but it cannot give the life or the power to obey that it demands. It is not that the law is evil, for it came with real glory; rather it belongs to a ministry that condemns, now surpassed by the Spirit who makes alive.

doxa.gloss: Glory, radiance, weighty splendour. The old covenant truly came with glory, seen in the shining of Moses' face, yet that glory was fading and had to be veiled. The glory of the new covenant surpasses it and endures, for it is the glory of the Lord Himself beheld with unveiled faces. This same glory grows in believers as they are changed into Christ's image from one degree of glory to the next.

metamorphoo.gloss: To transform, to change form, the word from which we get metamorphosis. It is used of Christ's transfiguration and of the renewing of the believer's mind in Romans 12:2. Here it describes the ongoing, Spirit wrought change of those who behold the Lord's glory with unveiled faces, so that they are progressively remade into His image with intensifying glory. It is passive: we are being transformed by the Lord, who is the Spirit, not by our own effort.

basic.context: Paul's opponents apparently carried letters of recommendation and questioned his credentials. Paul answers that he needs no such letter, for the Corinthian church itself, changed by the gospel, is his letter of recommendation, written by the Spirit of God on human hearts. This opens a rich comparison between the old covenant given through Moses and the new covenant of the Spirit, and shows how the glory that once shone on Moses' face is far surpassed by the glory now revealed in Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul is reading the account of Moses' shining and veiled face in Exodus 34 and drawing out its deeper meaning. He is not disparaging the law as evil; he calls it glorious. His point is comparative: a ministry that condemns is glorious, but a ministry that gives righteousness and the Spirit is far more glorious, and it endures where the old was fading. Read the whole passage as a contrast of two ministries, not two Gods or two Bibles.
basic.originalLanguages: The new covenant is diatheke, the arrangement God promised in Jeremiah 31. The contrast is between gramma, the written letter that kills, and pneuma, the Spirit who gives life. The old ministry had doxa, glory, but a fading glory, while the new has surpassing and enduring glory. And by the Spirit believers are transformed, metamorphoo, into Christ's image.
basic.typology: Moses with the veil over his shining face is the type; Christ and His unveiled people are the fulfilment. The old covenant engraved on tablets of stone foreshadows the new covenant written by the Spirit on hearts of flesh, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel promised. The fading glory of Sinai points forward to the abiding glory of the risen Lord beheld by faith.
basic.christ: Christ is the one in whom the veil is removed, the Lord to whom the heart turns and finds the covering taken away. He is the image of God into which believers are being transformed, and His glory is the glory now beheld with unveiled faces. The whole old covenant, rightly read, points to Him, and only in Him is it truly understood.
basic.god: God is the one who makes His servants competent, so that the ministry rests on His power and not on human ability. He is the living God who writes on human hearts by His Spirit, the God who keeps His covenant promise, and the God whose glory shines in the face of Christ. The Lord, the Spirit, brings freedom and transforms His people.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 31 promises the new covenant written on the heart. Ezekiel 36 promises a new heart and God's Spirit within. Exodus 34 records the shining and veiling of Moses' face. Romans 8 says the Spirit gives life where the law could not.
basic.oneStory: The Bible moves from a covenant written on stone that could command but not empower, to a new covenant in which God writes His law on the heart by His Spirit. Paul stands as a minister of that new covenant, and its glory, the glory of Christ, so surpasses the old that the fading radiance of Sinai is eclipsed. All who turn to the Lord have the veil lifted and are changed into His image.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as three arguments that grow out of one another. Verses 1 to 3 ask a question about credentials and answer it with a picture, the church as a letter. The picture of a letter written on tablets of the heart then calls up the other tablets, the stones of Sinai, and verses 4 to 11 turn into a comparison of two ministries. Verses 12 to 18 take up the one detail of the Sinai story Paul has not yet used, the veil, and make it do double work, first as a picture of a hardened Israel and then as a picture of every person who turns to the Lord.

The comparison in verses 7 to 11 is a chain of 'how much more' arguments, the kind of lesser to greater reasoning that rabbis later called qal wachomer. Paul states the same logic three times with different nouns: the ministry of death and the ministry of the Spirit, the ministry of condemnation and the ministry of righteousness, what was fading and what endures. The repetition is deliberate. Each pair gives the reader another word for what the old was and what the new is, and each leaves the old still glorious, only outshone.

A thread of word play runs through the chapter. Letters are read in verses 2 and 3, the old covenant is read in verses 14 and 15, and in verse 18 believers themselves are the ones who reflect. 'Glory' (doxa and its verb) is the word that keeps returning in verses 7 to 11 and again in verse 18. The verb translated 'fading away' returns in verses 7, 11, 13 and 14, giving the whole section its single leading idea, that glory can fade or abide. The chapter ends not with an argument but with a vision, the whole company of believers looking at the Lord with uncovered faces and being changed.
context.historical:
Letters of introduction were a regular part of travel in the Roman world, and a teacher arriving in a new city would often carry one from a figure the local people trusted. Paul's rivals in Corinth seem to have arrived with such letters, and they used them to make Paul's lack of one look suspect, 2 Corinthians 10:12 and 11:13. Paul does not reject the practice, since he himself sends letters of commendation, Romans 16:1-2. He rejects it as a replacement for evidence. The best proof of his ministry is the Corinthian church, as visible as a document everyone in the city can read.

Behind the comparison lies Sinai. Exodus tells us that after Moses had spent time with the LORD his face was radiant, that the people were afraid to come near, and that he put a veil over his face when he finished speaking to them, taking it off when he went in to speak with the LORD, Exodus 34:29-35. Those who heard Paul's letter were Gentile Christians but they had been taught the Scriptures of Israel, and they would have known the story either from synagogue connections or from Paul's own teaching.

The 'letter' in verse 6 is not the Old Testament as such. By 'the letter' Paul means the Law as a written code that demands what it cannot supply, a point he makes in Romans 7:6. The 'ministry of death' and 'ministry of condemnation' are descriptions of what the Law did, at Sinai itself, to a people who broke it within weeks, Exodus 32:28. Paul was himself a former Pharisee who knew what zeal for the written code looked like, and he writes with that experience behind him.
context.canonical:
This chapter is a meeting point of two promises. Jeremiah 31:31-34 foretold a new covenant, not like the one made at the exodus, in which God would put his law within his people and write it on their hearts. Ezekiel 36:26-27 promised a new heart and God's own Spirit within, so that his people would walk in his statutes. Paul says that both promises have arrived and that he is one of their servants. The letter written on hearts, verse 3, is Jeremiah, and 'the Spirit of the living God' is Ezekiel.

The chapter also stands on Exodus 34 and on the long Old Testament complaint about hardened hearts. Moses told Israel that the LORD had not yet given them a mind to understand, Deuteronomy 29:4, and Paul says the same condition still holds when the old covenant is read, verse 14. Romans 11:7-8 uses the same language of hardening and applies it to the people of Israel.

The theme returns across the New Testament. Romans 7:6 and 8:2-4 develop the contrast of the written code and the Spirit. Galatians 4:24-26 uses the figures of Hagar and Sarah for the two covenants. Hebrews 8:6-13 quotes Jeremiah 31 in full and argues that Jesus is the mediator of a better covenant. John 1:14 hears the glory of Sinai as an echo of the glory of the Word made flesh. Together these texts show that Paul's contrast is not his private view but a settled strand of New Testament teaching.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Corinthians to see why his ministry cannot be measured in the way his rivals measure it. If the ministry is a work of the Spirit that changes lives, then the right evidence is a changed life, not a reference. He wants them to look at themselves and see what God has done.

He also wants them to understand his boldness. Because the glory of the new covenant lasts, he can speak plainly. He has no need of a veil, no need to soften the message or conceal that the old arrangement has a limit. Behind this lies a pastoral concern: if the Corinthians fall back into measuring ministry by externals they will in effect return to the letter, and the very honour the Law once had will become a source of death.

The last verses are meant to lift the argument from defence to hope. A reader who sets the cost of ministry in 4:7 next to the vision of 3:18 will see that the ministry which looks small is in fact the means by which God remakes people into the likeness of Christ. Paul hopes the Corinthians will see their own lives that way too, as the place where the glory of the Lord is being shown and where they are being changed from one degree of glory to the next.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Paul's account of Moses' face is a reading of an old story, not a procedure to repeat. Nothing in the text asks believers to veil anything, and the verses about the veil do not address how Scripture is to be taught. They explain why the same Scripture can be read without being understood.

The statement that the letter kills is a theological description of what the Law does to sinners apart from the Spirit. It does not say that Christians are free to treat the commandments as irrelevant. In Romans 8:4 the righteous requirement of the Law is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit, and in Romans 7:12 the commandment is holy, righteous and good. The passage must be read with those verses beside it.

What this passage prescribes is a way of living. Turning to the Lord, verse 16, is the act that removes the veil, and it is never finished in a single moment; the participle in verse 18 describes continued beholding and continued change. Believers are told to look at him, not at their own progress, and to expect a gradual change that comes from the Lord. The freedom of verse 17 is not licence but release from the tyranny of the written demand, and it should not be used as a reason to ignore what God has said.

debates.question: In what sense does the letter kill?

views.label: The law reveals sin and pronounces condemnation
views.case: The written law exposes transgression and sentences the sinner to death, since it demands a righteousness it cannot supply; Romans 7 develops the same point, that the commandment meant for life brought death.

views.label: A merely external, literal religion apart from the Spirit
views.case: Some read letter and Spirit as two ways of relating to God: an outward, literalistic observance that deadens, versus inward life in the Spirit; this captures a real danger but risks blunting Paul's covenantal contrast.

debates.bearing: Either way the point stands that no written code can give life; life comes only through the Spirit of the new covenant, so the passage drives us from self effort to Christ.

debates.question: Does with unveiled faces reflect or behold the glory of the Lord?

views.label: Beholding as in a mirror
views.case: Many render it that believers contemplate the Lord's glory, and by that gazing are transformed, which fits the mirror imagery and the theme of turning to the Lord.

views.label: Reflecting the glory
views.case: Others take it that believers, like Moses, reflect the glory they have received, so that the transformation is also displayed outward; the BSB reads reflect.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that the glory is Christ's and the transformation is the Spirit's work; whether by beholding or reflecting, the believer is changed into the image of the Lord.

study.originalLanguages:
The word for 'fading away' in verses 7, 11, 13 and 14 is katargeo, a verb Paul uses often. It means to render inoperative, to bring to an end or to make of no effect, and it is the same verb that appears when he says that the last enemy, death, will be destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:26. In this chapter the sense is most naturally that the glory on Moses' face was passing away, and verse 13 says Moses covered his face so that Israel would not gaze to the end of that passing. The BSB's 'fleeting' in verse 7 and 'fading away' in verses 11 and 13 are fair choices, but the Greek is one word, and it is better to hear the same note through the whole chapter. A related question is whether Paul means that the old covenant itself passes away, or only its glory. The context speaks of the glory of the ministry, and Paul goes on to affirm the Law in Romans 3:31.

The four phrases beginning with 'the ministry of' in verses 7 to 9 all use diakonia. The ministry of death is diakonia tou thanatou, the ministry of condemnation is diakonia tes katakriseos, the ministry of righteousness is diakonia tes dikaiosynes, and the ministry of the Spirit is diakonia tou pneumatos. The genitives tell us what each ministry delivers. The old delivered death and condemnation, not because the Law was wicked but because it addressed sinners without being able to change them. The new delivers righteousness and the Spirit.

The 'letter' is gramma, a written character or code, as distinct from graphe, which is the word for Scripture as God's written word. Paul's usual word for Scripture is graphe, and he uses gramma for the written code as it stands alone, cut off from the Spirit. Romans 2:29 and 7:6 use the same word in the same way, which helps show he is not setting the Bible against the Spirit.

In verse 14 the minds of the Israelites 'were closed' translates eporothe, from the verb poroo, to harden or make dull. The same family of words appears in Romans 11:7, where the others 'were hardened,' and the passive voice leaves open who did the hardening. The passage does not say whether it is God, sin or the people, and it is wise to leave that question as open as Paul leaves it.

Verse 18 holds two of the passage's most discussed words. Katoptrizo comes from katoptron, a mirror, and can mean either 'to reflect as in a mirror' or 'to behold as in a mirror.' The BSB translates 'reflect.' The verb metamorphoo, 'transformed,' is the verb used of Jesus on the mountain, Matthew 17:2, and of the believer's renewing in Romans 12:2. 'From glory to glory' (apo doxes eis doxan) is a phrase of progress, and the BSB renders it 'with intensifying glory.' Those who look at the glory of the Lord become what they see.

typology.type: The tablets of stone, Exodus 31:18 and Deuteronomy 9:10
typology.fulfillment: The tablets written by the finger of God were the covenant's foundation and the centre of Israel's worship. Paul sets beside them the 'tablets of human hearts,' using language from Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26. In the new covenant the same God writes his law within his people, by the Spirit, Romans 8:4. Where the stone could set out the demand, the heart of flesh can receive and do it. The type is not rejected, since the commandments remain the standard. What the new covenant adds is the power to keep them, which stone could never give.

typology.type: Moses, mediator of the old covenant, Exodus 34:29-35
typology.fulfillment: Moses spoke with the LORD, came out radiant and brought the people a word. The pattern is a mediator who carries God's glory to the people. Paul sees in him a figure who falls short, because his radiance faded and he stood veiled in front of the people. Jesus mediates a better covenant, Hebrews 8:6, and he is the glory itself, not a reflection of it, John 1:14 and Hebrews 1:3. The type is true as far as it goes, since Moses really did bring God's word, but Christ goes beyond him by bringing us into the Lord's presence with an unveiled face.

typology.type: The veil over the face and the heart
typology.fulfillment: The veil on Moses' face becomes in verses 14 and 15 a veil over the hearts of those who hear Moses read without Christ. It is a picture of how a person can read the right words and miss the point. In Luke 24:27 and 24:45 the risen Jesus opens the Scriptures and opens his disciples' minds, and the veil is lifted by the one the Scriptures speak of. The correspondence is not exact, since Paul moves the veil from the face to the heart, and the passage should not be pressed into more detail than that.

The promise of an inward law and forgiveness of sins is the prophetic hope that stands behind the whole chapter. Hebrews 8:6-13 quotes the whole of it, and Jesus himself speaks of 'the new covenant in My blood' at the Supper, Luke 22:20. Paul serves as one of its ministers. The fulfilment is partial in one sense, since believers still wait for the full knowledge of the Lord that Jeremiah describes, but the Spirit is already given as the first instalment, 2 Corinthians 1:22.

study.christ:
Christ is the hinge of this chapter, and Paul says so three times. The letter on the Corinthians' hearts is 'a letter from Christ,' verse 3. The veil is lifted only 'in Christ,' verse 14. And in verse 16 the person to whom a heart turns is 'the Lord.' To see how the whole argument depends on him, consider each of these in turn.

The Corinthians are Christ's letter because he is the one who writes. Their transformation is not a result of Paul's skill but of the risen Lord at work through the Spirit. That claim matters because it tells us where to look for Christ today, not only in a record of what he did but in a changed people, and it is the opposite of the notion that Christ has withdrawn from the world.

The veil comes off in Christ because he is the meaning of the old covenant. The risen Jesus taught that the whole of Moses and the Prophets spoke of him, Luke 24:27, and Paul says that Christ is the end, the goal, of the Law, Romans 10:4. The Greek word there can mean end or goal, and in context both senses are present: the Law reaches its aim in him and its condemning role ceases for those who are in him. This means a person can read Exodus with every detail in view and still miss what it is about until Christ is seen.

The glory itself is Christ's. Moses saw something of the glory of the LORD and was changed on the outside for a time. John says of the Word made flesh, 'We have seen His glory,' John 1:14, and Paul says two verses after our passage that the light of the knowledge of the glory of God is 'in the face of Jesus Christ,' 2 Corinthians 4:6. What Moses reflected for a season, Christ possesses permanently. So believers are not looking at a fading light but at the face of the one who is the image of God, 4:4 and Colossians 1:15.

The last strand is the work of the Spirit. The Spirit is called 'the Spirit of the Lord' in verse 17 and 'the Lord, who is the Spirit' in verse 18, so Christ and the Spirit are bound together in this work of transformation. Paul calls Christ the last Adam, who became a life-giving spirit, 1 Corinthians 15:45, and Jesus said that the words he spoke are spirit and life, John 6:63. The new covenant ministry gives life because the Lord who is the Spirit gives it.

A caution applies. This passage should not be turned into a claim that Moses, or the Jews who read him today, are somehow outside God's care. Paul himself grieves for Israel and hopes for their turning, Romans 9:1-5 and 11:25-27. The veil is a problem to be removed by Christ, not a condemnation to be pronounced from a distance.
study.god:
The chapter begins and ends with God as the one who acts. He writes the letter, qualifies the ministers, gives the Spirit and works the change in us. Almost every verb of real significance has God or the Spirit as its source: the letter is written 'with the Spirit of the living God,' verse 3, competence 'comes from God,' verse 5, 'He has qualified us,' verse 6, and the glory 'comes from the Lord,' verse 18. Paul's confidence rests on this, not on himself.

God is the living God. The phrase in verse 3 sets him against the dead stone of tablets and against the idols of Corinth, and it describes the God who speaks and acts. When God writes, what he writes is alive, and the text on the heart is not archived but active.

He is consistent with himself. The ministry of the old covenant was glorious, and Paul does not deny it. The same God gave both covenants, and the glory of Sinai was real. This shows that God's later works do not make his earlier ones false, only fuller. He is also a God who keeps promises across centuries, since Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant was made hundreds of years before this letter, and Paul reads it as now being kept.

He is a God of both holiness and freedom. The Sinai glory was so intense that the people could not look at Moses, and the account in Exodus 33:20 says that no one can see his face and live. Yet Paul says that believers look at the glory of the Lord with unveiled faces. The holiness has not been reduced; the way to it has been opened by Christ. God is not lowered to meet us. We are brought to him. That is the grace of the new covenant.

God is also the Giver of freedom, verse 17. Where his Spirit is, there is freedom, a theme Paul develops in Galatians 5:1 and Romans 8:2. Freedom here is not independence from God but release from condemnation and from the weight of an external code, so that we can live from the heart.

He is a patient God, working in people by degrees. The transformation of verse 18 is continuous and takes a lifetime, and it is done by the Lord himself. He does not demand perfection and then wait to see whether we produce it. He works the change as we look to him.

For worship, the passage teaches us to look. Believers do not stand before God as the Israelites stood before Moses, afraid and at a distance. They come with an unveiled face to the glory of the Lord, and the right response is to keep looking, with gratitude, and to let him do the work of changing us.

crossReferences.note: The promise behind verses 3 and 6. God says the new covenant will not be like the one he made at the exodus, a covenant the people broke, and that he will put his law within them and write it on their hearts. Paul says that this is now being carried out through his ministry.

The promise of a heart of flesh in place of a heart of stone, and of God's own Spirit within his people so that they walk in his statutes. It supplies the contrast between stone and heart in 2 Corinthians 3:3, and shows that the Spirit's work is what makes obedience possible.

The story Paul reinterprets. Moses came down with his face radiant, the people feared to approach, and he wore a veil except when he went in to speak with the LORD. Reading it first shows how carefully Paul has chosen the details he uses, and how much he leaves out.

Moses told Israel that to that day the LORD had not given them a mind to understand, eyes to see or ears to hear. It is the Old Testament source of the idea of a hardened mind in verse 14, and shows that the veil is a problem the Law itself already recognised.

Believers have been released from the law so that they serve in the new way of the Spirit and not in the old way of the written code. It is the closest parallel to 'not of the letter but of the Spirit' and shows that Paul's contrast is a settled theme, not a passing phrase.

The law of the Spirit of life sets believers free from the law of sin and death, and the righteous requirement of the law is fulfilled in those who walk by the Spirit. It explains how the letter can kill and yet the law remain good: the Spirit does what the written code could not.

Quotes Jeremiah 31 at length and argues that Jesus mediates a better covenant founded on better promises. It treats the same passage as 2 Corinthians 3 and arrives at the same conclusion by a different route, which suggests that this reading was common in the early church.

Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes. It gives the key to 2 Corinthians 3:14, where the veil is removed only in Christ. The law's purpose is reached in him, and those who hold to the law without him miss its point.

The next chapter takes the language of glory and sight further. Christ is the image of God, and God has made his light shine in our hearts to give the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ. It is the full statement of what the unveiled face of 3:18 sees.

Now we see in a mirror dimly, then face to face. It uses the same mirror word as 2 Corinthians 3:18, and shows that the beholding of this age is real but partial, and that the full sight is still to come when the change will be complete.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward the Bible tells of a God who wants to dwell with his people and of people who cannot bear his presence. Adam hid among the trees. At Sinai the people begged Moses to speak to them in place of God, Exodus 20:19, and when Moses came down with his face shining they were afraid to approach, Exodus 34:30. The veil is one small picture of a larger gap. God is glorious, and sinners cannot look at him and live.

The covenants try to bridge that gap. God makes promises to Abraham, gives the law through Moses and builds the tabernacle, but each time the story shows that something more is needed. The prophets name what that is. Jeremiah promises a covenant in which God himself writes the law within, and Ezekiel promises a new heart and a new Spirit. The problem is not that God's word is weak but that human hearts are hard, and only God can change them.

In this chapter that promise is declared to have arrived. The old ministry came with glory and led to death, and Paul does not deny either part. The new ministry gives righteousness and life by the Spirit, and its glory does not fade. The way to the face of God, closed since Eden, has been opened in Christ.

Looking forward, verse 18 is the first description of the whole Christian life as a work of re-creation. Humanity was made in the image of God, Genesis 1:27, and the fall defaced that image. Now Christ, who is the true image, is restoring it in his people by degrees, and the work will be finished when we see him. John writes that when he appears we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is, 1 John 3:2.

The story ends in Revelation 22:4, where God's servants will see his face and his name will be on their foreheads. The veil that Moses wore, and that hung in the temple, and that lay over the hearts of those who heard Moses read, is gone for good. What Paul begins to describe in Corinth, an unveiled face turned toward the Lord and a people being changed, is the shape of the new creation seen from within.

quiz.q: What did Paul mean by calling the Corinthians his letter of recommendation?

options.text: Their changed lives, written by the Spirit on human hearts, proved the truth of his ministry.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 make the church itself the living evidence, written by the Spirit.

options.text: They had physically written him a glowing reference to carry.
options.note: Paul means a living letter of transformed lives, not an actual written reference.

options.text: They had recommended him to other churches by mail.
options.note: The point is what the Spirit wrote in them, not correspondence they sent.

options.text: He needed their approval before he could preach.
options.note: Paul's confidence comes from God, not from human approval.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean when he says the letter kills but the Spirit gives life?

options.text: The written law reveals sin and condemns, but the Spirit of the new covenant gives life.
options.note: Verse 6 contrasts the condemning law with the life giving Spirit.

options.text: The Old Testament is bad and only the New Testament is good.
options.note: Paul calls the old ministry glorious; he contrasts covenants, not good and evil books.

options.text: We should ignore the commandments entirely.
options.note: The law is holy; the point is that it cannot give the life it demands.
Paul is not warning against Scripture but explaining law and Spirit.

quiz.q: How does the glory of the new covenant compare to the old?

options.text: It surpasses and outlasts it; the old glory was real but fading, the new endures.
options.note: Verses 7 to 11 argue from lesser to greater that the new glory surpasses and endures.

options.text: The old covenant had no glory at all.
options.note: Paul insists the old ministry did come with glory, only a fading one.

options.text: They are exactly equal in glory.
options.note: Paul stresses how much greater the new covenant glory is.

options.text: The new covenant has less glory than the old.
options.note: The whole argument is that the new glory is far greater.

quiz.q: According to verse 18, how are believers transformed into the image of Christ?

options.text: By the Spirit, as with unveiled faces they behold the glory of the Lord.
options.note: The transformation is the Spirit's work as we behold the Lord's glory.

options.text: By trying harder to imitate Jesus in their own strength.
options.note: The verb is passive; the Lord, the Spirit, transforms us as we behold Him.

options.text: All at once, the moment they believe, with nothing ongoing.
options.note: It is a progressive change, from one degree of glory to another.

options.text: By keeping the law engraved on stone.
options.note: The law could not give life; transformation comes by the Spirit in Christ.

questions: Paul pointed to changed lives as proof of real ministry. What in your life would show that the Spirit has been writing on your heart?
The law can tell us what is right but cannot give us power to do it. Where are you relying on rules or self effort instead of the life giving Spirit?
Paul says the glory of the old covenant, real as it was, faded before the greater glory of Christ. What lesser glories are you tempted to cling to that keep you from Christ's greater glory?
The veil is removed when a person turns to the Lord. Is there any area where your heart is still veiled, where you need to turn afresh to Christ?
We are changed into Christ's image by beholding His glory. What practical habits help you behold the Lord, and how might you give more time to gazing on Him?

translationNotes.note: The letter kills but the Spirit gives life contrasts gramma, the written code of the old covenant, with the pneuma, the Holy Spirit of the new; it is a contrast of covenants and ministries, not a claim that the law is evil.

Now the Lord is the Spirit identifies the Lord of the Exodus narrative with the Spirit at work in the new covenant; it affirms the Spirit's deity and His life giving, freeing work, without collapsing the distinction of the divine persons.
The verb rendered reflect can also be rendered behold as in a mirror; both readings agree the glory is the Lord's and the transformation, metamorphoo, is the Spirit's work in the believer.
